title: Alchemy
objective: After this level you can explain what alchemists tried to do and what they got right.
summary: Alchemists chased gold and long life and never caught either. Along the way they built the tools of the lab, like the alembic still, and gave chemistry its very name.

cards.headline: Isaac Newton wrote about a million words on alchemy.
cards.body: The man who explained gravity spent some thirty years on it, mostly in secret. So what were alchemists chasing, and was any of it worth the effort?

cards.headline: The dream: gold, and a longer life
cards.body: Alchemists tried to turn base metals, such as lead or copper, into silver or gold. Many hoped to make the philosophers' stone, a material that was supposed to do the transforming for them. A second dream ran alongside: a cure for disease and a way to extend life. Big goals. As it turned out, what they built while chasing them mattered far more.

cards.headline: The toolkit they left behind
cards.body: Alchemists described apparatus for distillation, sublimation and filtration in careful detail. Their alembic was a still in three parts: a vessel to heat the mixture, a head to catch and cool the vapor, and a receiver for the liquid that dripped out. Remember Level 7? Distilling works because the parts of a mixture boil at different temperatures. Three Chapter 1 moves were already on the alchemist's bench.

mascot.line: Level 7's distilling, in an alchemist's still. They had the right moves and the wrong prize.

cards.headline: Words that stuck around
cards.body: The word alchemy comes from the Arabic al-kimiya, and the word chemistry grew out of alchemy. Arabic alchemy handed down alcohol, elixir and alembic too. And an ancient alchemist named Maria is credited with gentle heating in a bath of hot water instead of an open flame. Her name survives in the cook's bain-marie. The gold never came. The lab did.
cards.callout: Chemistry's name, tools and techniques all passed through the alchemist's workshop.

questions.prompt: Alchemists hoped to transform base metals like lead and copper. Into what?

options.label: Glass or pottery
options.rationale: Glassmaking and pottery were never the alchemists' goal.

options.label: Salt or pure water
options.rationale: Those weren't the prize; precious metals were.

questions.explanation: Alchemists tried to transform base metals such as lead or copper into silver or gold, hoping for a philosophers' stone to do it.

questions.prompt: Alchemists never made gold. Why do historians still give them a place in the story of chemistry?

options.label: They proved that gold can never be made by chemistry
options.rationale: They kept trying; proving it impossible wasn't their work.

options.label: They wrote the first table of all the elements
They built lab tools and techniques like distillation
They discovered that air has mass and weight

questions.explanation: Their apparatus for distilling, subliming and filtering, like the alembic, became part of the chemist's toolkit.

questions.prompt: The alchemist's alembic was a still. From Level 7, why can distilling separate the parts of a mixture?

options.label: The parts boil at different temperatures
The parts have different colors
options.rationale: Color doesn't decide what turns to vapor first.

options.label: A filter inside holds back the solids
Heat turns every part into gold

questions.explanation: Distillation heats a mixture and collects the vapor; the part with the lowest boiling point comes off first.
